questiontext.text:
Goal

A night sentry records each patrol by signing a gate book on entry and again on exit. The sentry must always sign out after entering. A name missing from the roster never enters, so it needs no exit signature. A post recorded as breach ends the patrol before the sentry checks it, and the sentry still signs out. The patrol then reports the error breach at post 2 when the breach is the second post, counted from 1.

Read
  • Defer, Panic, and Recover. Read the first three paragraphs. What does a defer statement save? When do the saved calls run?
  • In the second CopyFile listing, which comes first for each file, the error check or the defer?
  • Read the three numbered rules. Which rule defines when a deferred call runs? Does an early return change that timing?
Coming from Java

The reflex is a finally clause wrapped around the whole patrol, or try-with-resources on the gate. Go has no try and no finally, and signIn and signOut are plain functions.

signIn(name);
try {
    for (String post : posts) { ... }
} finally {
    signOut(name);
}
Required: defer
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Trace the CopyFile path where os.Open fails. Does execution reach defer src.Close()?
  • Count the return statements in patrol. Apply the second numbered rule to each one.

testcode.text: err := patrol("Ada", []string{"east gate", "north wall"}) fmt.Println(err == nil)

expected.text: Ada on duty checking east gate checking north wall Ada off duty true
Cy on duty Cy off duty true
Bo on duty checking east gate Bo off duty breach at post 2

testcode.text: err := patrol("", []string{"east gate"}) fmt.Println(err == ErrNoName) fmt.Println(patrol("Di", []string{"breach"}))

expected.text: true Di on duty Di off duty breach at post 1

questiontext.text:
Goal

A dead-end storage shed has one door, so the last parade float inside must leave first. The foreman also runs a dispatch where each float enters and leaves before the next arrives. parade returns the number of floats standing in the shed as its return statement runs. That count includes its own floats and any float parked before the call. A float named stall turns back at the door, so parade sends in nothing after it and returns at once.

Read
  • Defer statements. Find the paragraph beginning "Each time a defer statement executes". When are the call's parameters evaluated? In what order do deferred calls run?
  • In the sentence beginning "That is", does an explicit return set result parameters before or after deferred calls run?
  • Inspect the code example. What does its loop print? Does anything print while the loop is running?
Coming from Java

The reflex is try-with-resources inside the loop body, so the block releases each float at the end of its own iteration. Read the linked paragraph on when a deferred call runs before you copy that shape.

for (String name : floats) {
    try (Slot slot = depot.enter(name)) {
        ...
    }
}
Required: defer
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • leave refuses a float that is not at the door, so compare the order your calls run in against the sentence on order.
  • If dispatch prints every entry before any exit, reread which function a deferred call waits for.

expected.text: Brass Band enters Dragon enters Fire Engine enters Fire Engine leaves Dragon leaves Brass Band leaves
Brass Band enters Brass Band leaves Dragon enters Dragon leaves
Brass Band enters Dragon enters Fire Engine enters Fire Engine leaves Dragon leaves Brass Band leaves 3 0

testcode.text: d := &Depot{} d.enter("Mayor") dispatch(d, []string{"Dragon"}) fmt.Println(parade(d, nil), len(d.inside)) fmt.Println(parade(d, []string{"Fire Engine"}), len(d.inside)) d.leave("Mayor")

expected.text: Mayor enters Dragon enters Dragon leaves 1 1 Fire Engine enters Fire Engine leaves 2 1 Mayor leaves
Brass Band enters Brass Band leaves 1 0

questiontext.text:
Goal

A matching engine processes trading orders one at a time. Another team wrote the engine, and a bad order makes it panic. Record that failure and continue with the remaining orders. A failed order takes the error's own text as its line in the list session returns. quote applies the engine's price rule and never panics. It returns 0 with unknown symbol ZZZ for a symbol not in the book and zero quantity for AAPL for a quantity of 0.

Read
  • Handling panics. Find the paragraph beginning "Suppose a function G defers a function D". After D returns normally, what happens to G? Where does execution resume?
  • In the next paragraph, which two situations make recover return nil?
  • Defer, Panic, and Recover. Find the paragraph about the json package. What does its external API return when the package uses panic internally?
Coming from Java

The reflex is a try block around the engine call and a catch that carries on inside the same method. Read the linked section on where execution resumes before you copy that shape.

try {
    cost = engine.price(book, order);
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    return new Fill(0, "fill " + order.symbol() + ": " + e.getMessage());
}
Banned: nakedreturn. Required: recover
Stuck? Two nudges inside
  • Find the spec's protect example, then compare where its call to recover sits with where yours sits.
  • settle runs on every fill, successful ones included, so reread the paragraph on when recover returns nil.

testcode.text: book := map[string]int{"AAPL": 150, "MSFT": 400} cost, err := fill(book, Order{Symbol: "AAPL", Qty: 2}) fmt.Println(cost, err == nil) cost, err = fill(book, Order{Symbol: "MSFT", Qty: 0}) fmt.Println(cost, err)

expected.text: 312 true 0 fill MSFT: runtime error: integer divide by zero
true fill BOOM: engine down AAPL x4 = 612 fill ZZZ: unknown symbol ZZZ fill MSFT: runtime error: integer divide by zero MSFT x1 = 412 0 zero quantity for MSFT 0 unknown symbol ZZZ 612 true
